entries.title: Thinkers of Cernavodă: Mysterious Stone Age figurines discovered in a 7,000-year-old grave in Romania
entries.caption:
🗿 Romania’s 7,000-year-old “Thinkers” are still a mystery.

Live Science reports that archaeologists uncovered the fired-clay pair in 1956 in a Stone Age grave at Cernavodă. One figure leans forward with his head in his hands; the other sits upright. Both are associated with the Late Neolithic Hamangia culture, around 5000 B.C.

Their purpose remains uncertain. Interpretations range from ritual or solar symbolism to mourners or a paired representation of masculine and feminine principles. None is confirmed.

Why do you think these small figures still feel so modern?

Source: Live Science (16 Nov 2026)
https://www.livescience.com/archaeology/thinkers-of-cernavoda-mysterious-stone-age-figurines-discovered-in-a-7-000-year-old-grave-in-romania

entries.title: Medieval Readers Saw Floods, Plagues and Comets as Omens of Doom—So They Created a Mysterious Manuscript of Apocalyptic Artworks to Peruse at Will
entries.caption:
Medieval readers confronting plagues and floods apparently sought solace in the terrifying art of "The Book of Miracles," a 16th-century manuscript slated for auction according to Smithsonian Smart News on November 18, 2026. This rare artifact, likely created in Augsburg, reportedly features 167 distinct paintings depicting extreme weather events and strange celestial phenomena. While scholars suggest these apocalyptic artworks served as omens of doom to be perused at will, the exact motivations of its original creators remain partially shrouded in history. Could such vivid historical expressions of collective anxiety offer unexpected comfort to modern readers facing their own unprecedented global uncertainties?

Source: Smithsonian Smart News · 18 Nov 2026
https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/medieval-readers-saw-floods-plagues-and-comets-as-omens-of-doom-so-they-created-a-mysterious-manuscript-of-apocalyptic-artworks-to-peruse-at-will-180989891/

entries.title: Tiny dog. Wild ancestry.
entries.caption:
Tiny dog, unexpected family history. 🐕

A genetic study found traces of coyote ancestry in Chihuahuas, estimated at roughly 0.1% of their genome. The link appears to come from interbreeding between coyotes and ancestors of domestic dogs long ago.

That does not mean a Chihuahua is a miniature coyote. Researchers say this small genetic contribution probably does not explain the breed’s bold personality. More research is needed to pin down the ancestral connection.

Source: Smithsonian · 18 Nov 2026
https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/chihuahuas-seem-to-carry-a-tiny-bit-of-coyote-dna-but-thats-probably-not-why-they-have-fearless-personalities-180989886/

entries.title: Scientists put 78,000 letters of human DNA into a mouse — and unraveled how a rare disease worked
entries.caption:
By inserting human genes into lab mice, researchers have reportedly unraveled the underlying mechanics of a rare disease that has proven notoriously difficult to study. According to Live Science on November 21, 2026, the scientific team successfully put 78,000 letters of human DNA into a mouse model to better understand the condition. While the experiment provides a new window into these complex biological processes, it remains to be seen how effectively this humanized mouse model will translate to future human treatments.

Source: Live Science · 21 Nov 2026
https://www.livescience.com/health/genetics/scientists-put-78-000-letters-of-human-dna-into-a-mouse-and-unraveled-how-a-rare-disease-worked

entries.title: Have Archaeologists Finally Pieced Together the 'Parthenon Puzzle,' One of Ancient Greece's Greatest Mysteries?
entries.caption:
German researchers reportedly believe they have solved one of ancient Greece's greatest mysteries by digitally piecing together the shattered east pediment of the Parthenon. Smithsonian Smart News reports that centuries after the monument's renowned sculptural scene was reduced to rubble, the team used modern 3D printers and Roman sarcophagi to recreate the intricate 39-figure depiction of Athena's birth. While this innovative approach offers a compelling glimpse into antiquity, experts emphasize that these digital and physical models represent a calculated hypothesis rather than a confirmed recreation of the lost original artifacts. How close can modern technology truly bring us to restoring history's most fragile masterpieces?

Source: Smithsonian Smart News · 19 Nov 2026
https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/have-archaeologists-finally-pieced-together-the-parthenon-puzzle-one-of-ancient-greece-greatest-mysteries-180989903/

entries.title: An ancient failed rift is reawakening inside one of Africa's oldest landmasses
entries.caption:
An unexpected seismic jolt deep within one of Africa's most ancient continental cores has geologists rethinking the stability of the Earth's oldest landmasses. In April 2017, a magnitude 6.5 earthquake unexpectedly struck the middle of the Kalahari Craton in eastern Botswana, according to recent reports. Scientists previously considered this region, built from blocks of crust up to 3.7 billion years old, far too cold, thick, and rigid to tear apart. Researchers indicate that this rare event suggests an ancient failed rift inside the craton may be reawakening. Could other supposedly stable continental cores be harboring hidden tectonic activity?

Source: Phys.org Earth · 21 Nov 2026
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ancient-rift-reawakening-africa-oldest.html

entries.title: Robot submarine exploring world's deepest ocean trench finds unprecedented volcanic activity
entries.caption:
An autonomous robotic submarine plumbing the crushing depths of the Mariana Trench has reportedly uncovered evidence of unprecedented, deep-sea volcanic activity. According to Phys.org Earth reports published on November 23, 2026, researchers seeking to understand how the abyss reached its nearly 11,000-meter depth deployed a remotely operated vehicle to gather samples. The source text states that this machine ultimately discovered traces of what is described as the world's deepest underwater explosive event, stemming from a geological history where the Pacific tectonic plate began sliding beneath the Philippine Sea plate 52 million years ago. However, as ongoing investigations continue, scientists have yet to fully explain all the mechanisms behind this extreme topography. What secrets might future robotic dives reveal about the violent forces shaping Earth's most extreme environments?

Source: Phys.org Earth · 23 Nov 2026
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-robot-submarine-exploring-world-deepest.html

entries.title: A tomb with distant connections
entries.caption:
A glass cup believed to be Roman was among 413 artifacts found in a roughly 2,000-year-old Xiongnu tomb in Mongolia. The jade objects, silver pendant and other finds add evidence of far-reaching exchange networks, but they do not reveal the cup's exact journey or prove direct contact between Rome and Mongolia.

Source: Smithsonian Smart News · 20 Nov 2026

entries.title: A second chance for a rare snake
entries.caption:
A bright snake gets a head start. Conservationists released 62 young San Francisco garter snakes after raising them for about a year, giving the endangered animals a better chance of surviving their vulnerable early months. The release supports a wider recovery effort; it does not mean the species has recovered. Exact locations are withheld to protect the snakes.

Source: Smithsonian Smart News · 23 Nov 2026

entries.title: A tiny flower hidden for 100 million years
entries.caption:
Micro-CT X-rays revealed a tiny flower hidden inside a sandstone museum specimen collected in Kansas more than 130 years ago. The roughly 100-million-year-old flower survives as a negative cavity left after the original material decayed. Its structure may point to an extinct palm relative, but that classification remains uncertain.

Source: Phys.org / Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew · 23 Nov 2026
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-hidden-million-years-rays-reveal.html

entries.title: The golden burbot
entries.caption:
Most burbot blend into the lake bottom with mottled brown and olive coloring. During a survey of New York’s Oswego Harbor, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service biologists caught one in vivid yellow-orange. The unusual coloring comes from xanthochromism, a rare condition that lets yellow pigment dominate. Burbot are native to the Great Lakes, and this was the first recorded burbot in a fisheries survey of that harbor.

Source: Smithsonian Smart News · 24 Nov 2026
https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/biologists-discovere-a-one-in-a-million-bright-yellow-burbot-fish-in-new-yorks-oswego-harbor-180989928/
